$F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}+1,\,{y}^{2}⟩$
across the triangle $C$ with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),$ and $(0,2)$ can be represented as

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C,$ and $D$ is the region bounded by $C.$ Calculate the function $f(x,y).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/c3/c3c617522488e6ebf47dd2b2a52c43a1fe06ccaef8cd1e8752ab4df5e2d4bd64.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+1$ and $Q(x,y)={y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=2(x+y).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168711 :answer-field/correct "answer-9d5ab6e6-3ed2-5325-ad32-339384996043" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9d5ab6e6-3ed2-5325-ad32-339384996043" "answer-ae24f312-5321-5cc9-87dd-f8625d1a40c3" "answer-e838f00f-7aa2-51c0-8734-9a7dc0bd6c20" "answer-b7765c6a-5ae2-501d-ad46-c25d34ebcac5" "answer-6730175f-e2ca-5f18-8300-20f526084f78"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9d5ab6e6-3ed2-5325-ad32-339384996043" :answer/id #uuid "9d5ab6e6-3ed2-5325-ad32-339384996043" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2(x+y)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ae24f312-5321-5cc9-87dd-f8625d1a40c3" :answer/id #uuid "ae24f312-5321-5cc9-87dd-f8625d1a40c3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2(x-y)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e838f00f-7aa2-51c0-8734-9a7dc0bd6c20" :answer/id #uuid "e838f00f-7aa2-51c0-8734-9a7dc0bd6c20" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2(y-x)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b7765c6a-5ae2-501d-ad46-c25d34ebcac5" :answer/id #uuid "b7765c6a-5ae2-501d-ad46-c25d34ebcac5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6730175f-e2ca-5f18-8300-20f526084f78" :answer/id #uuid "6730175f-e2ca-5f18-8300-20f526084f78" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-dccc7f7f-0cab-5758-b1da-5b22069d8a23" :question/id #uuid "dccc7f7f-0cab-5758-b1da-5b22069d8a23" :question/math-academy-id "q-127203" :question/problem "According to the flux form of Green's theorem, the flux of the vector field

$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C,$ and $D$ is the region bounded by $C.$ Calculate the function $f(x,y).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}={y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({y}^{2}+(-{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=6xy+y{x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=-{y}^{2}.$ So,  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=6y+2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2y.\end{aligned}

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 2\}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(6y+2xy)+(-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2}2y(2+x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-17417f10-d5b1-59a3-bbd0-62b09d7aaa49"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C,$ and $D$ is the region bounded by $C.$ Calculate the function $f(x,y).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/f1/f1b9472021d3973167a7601785803837627476a4e8b1460e42f87e91ecb99d7e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{3}+{y}^{3}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =3{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-501779b1-729b-5f0b-8f00-ddfd19deba04"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-501779b1-729b-5f0b-8f00-ddfd19deba04" :answer-field/id #uuid "501779b1-729b-5f0b-8f00-ddfd19deba04" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ac21a517-9ce2-51e1-a210-d1342e658153" :answer-field/choices ["answer-84832c07-1cf7-5890-95f5-93379bbcf9e7" "answer-ac21a517-9ce2-51e1-a210-d1342e658153" "answer-a513c7fb-0fe0-56ce-955a-00f68e2e1226" "answer-eb98dc31-4f54-5896-a0d6-e621b6d1e1f7" "answer-036be383-69ad-5c54-97f4-245cc64ebdc5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-84832c07-1cf7-5890-95f5-93379bbcf9e7" :answer/id #uuid "84832c07-1cf7-5890-95f5-93379bbcf9e7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ac21a517-9ce2-51e1-a210-d1342e658153" :answer/id #uuid "ac21a517-9ce2-51e1-a210-d1342e658153" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a513c7fb-0fe0-56ce-955a-00f68e2e1226" :answer/id #uuid "a513c7fb-0fe0-56ce-955a-00f68e2e1226" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eb98dc31-4f54-5896-a0d6-e621b6d1e1f7" :answer/id #uuid "eb98dc31-4f54-5896-a0d6-e621b6d1e1f7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-036be383-69ad-5c54-97f4-245cc64ebdc5" :answer/id #uuid "036be383-69ad-5c54-97f4-245cc64ebdc5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5645d046-8b12-5960-a3e0-e0429413dd27" :question/id #uuid "5645d046-8b12-5960-a3e0-e0429413dd27" :question/math-academy-id "q-127337" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{y}^{7}-x,\,{e}^{3x}+x{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the rectangle with vertices $(-1,-1),(0,-1),(0,1),$ and $(-1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/b2/b25d12781632bcc03576a79e7fbf1b22806fc68e3f521ecd602f1b0732d8d90d.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={y}^{7}-x$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{3x}+x{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 0,\,-1\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+2xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(2xy-1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}y-x)\,{|}_{-1}^{0}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[0-((-1)^{2}y-(-1))]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-y-1)\,dy \\  & =[-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-y]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-\frac{(1)^{2}}{2}-(1))-(-\frac{(-1)^{2}}{2}-(-1)) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-15f3b20c-fcac-5124-a093-6cfd6cef919f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-15f3b20c-fcac-5124-a093-6cfd6cef919f" :answer-field/id #uuid "15f3b20c-fcac-5124-a093-6cfd6cef919f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-783926e4-15e5-52ff-ad59-711ade6b214d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-db270bba-95df-51f5-b9d1-ccab96038132" "answer-783926e4-15e5-52ff-ad59-711ade6b214d" "answer-9ceb053a-ae1f-53f2-9912-d9d9157552fa" "answer-5ebdbb3a-9cd8-57c7-9768-3437a54bb5b2" "answer-1afc0e4b-7ec3-5e04-a320-b09bbb7450d5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-db270bba-95df-51f5-b9d1-ccab96038132" :answer/id #uuid "db270bba-95df-51f5-b9d1-ccab96038132" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-783926e4-15e5-52ff-ad59-711ade6b214d" :answer/id #uuid "783926e4-15e5-52ff-ad59-711ade6b214d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9ceb053a-ae1f-53f2-9912-d9d9157552fa" :answer/id #uuid "9ceb053a-ae1f-53f2-9912-d9d9157552fa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5ebdbb3a-9cd8-57c7-9768-3437a54bb5b2" :answer/id #uuid "5ebdbb3a-9cd8-57c7-9768-3437a54bb5b2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1afc0e4b-7ec3-5e04-a320-b09bbb7450d5" :answer/id #uuid "1afc0e4b-7ec3-5e04-a320-b09bbb7450d5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172305 :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}+2y,\,{x}^{2}+2xy⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{2}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/91/9168d2ed7eeaa5f1dd331a0a986ac7ecfd6b964217a2cb614deb0cdd54437d65.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+2y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+2xy.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}4x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4xy\,{|}_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{x}^{3}\,dx \\  & ={x}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & ={1}^{4}-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168693 :answer-field/correct 17592186168696 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-380026fe-2d4e-5527-8902-7fe90302976f" :question/id #uuid "380026fe-2d4e-5527-8902-7fe90302976f" :question/math-academy-id "q-127302" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨14xy,\,6{x}^{2}y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{3}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/e6/e6f6a5cf9b37fe16f17fe74face946d85b426badf8db710ca4a7ea308a1ff2ec.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=14xy$ and $Q(x,y)=6{x}^{2}y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=14y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =6{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{3}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(14y+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}(14y+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7{y}^{2}+6{x}^{2}y)\,{|}_{0}^{{x}^{3}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7{x}^{6}+6{x}^{5})\,dx \\  & =({x}^{7}+{x}^{6})\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1f5abcf2-857d-5997-8843-79c2143f0e91"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1f5abcf2-857d-5997-8843-79c2143f0e91" :answer-field/id #uuid "1f5abcf2-857d-5997-8843-79c2143f0e91" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-be728807-7dfc-57ad-844a-74242eaae230" :answer-field/choices ["answer-be728807-7dfc-57ad-844a-74242eaae230" "answer-f65df826-8fea-532c-b10f-fd1044e7f4a0" "answer-9e8a5a99-44bd-5b11-83dd-6c16e9e4e40b" "answer-f1954043-6aaa-5ee4-807d-74a521f1268a" "answer-a581e533-3d41-5f80-8a3e-7a4d97fd2b2b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-be728807-7dfc-57ad-844a-74242eaae230" :answer/id #uuid "be728807-7dfc-57ad-844a-74242eaae230" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f65df826-8fea-532c-b10f-fd1044e7f4a0" :answer/id #uuid "f65df826-8fea-532c-b10f-fd1044e7f4a0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9e8a5a99-44bd-5b11-83dd-6c16e9e4e40b" :answer/id #uuid "9e8a5a99-44bd-5b11-83dd-6c16e9e4e40b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f1954043-6aaa-5ee4-807d-74a521f1268a" :answer/id #uuid "f1954043-6aaa-5ee4-807d-74a521f1268a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{6}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a581e533-3d41-5f80-8a3e-7a4d97fd2b2b" :answer/id #uuid "a581e533-3d41-5f80-8a3e-7a4d97fd2b2b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172304 :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨3{x}^{5}+2y,\,3{y}^{2}-{e}^{x}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,1),$ and $(-1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/26/269e3c7f92cee66c78f3226e7c967eb51153503c598d2e4d1e4b56a33e646ac4.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=3{x}^{5}+2y$ and $Q(x,y)=3{y}^{2}-{e}^{x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=15{x}^{4},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =6y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(15{x}^{4}+6y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y}^{y}(15{x}^{4}+6y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[3{x}^{5}+6xy]_{-y}^{y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[(3{y}^{5}+6{y}^{2})-(-3{y}^{5}-6{y}^{2})]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6{y}^{5}+12{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & =[{y}^{6}+4{y}^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+4)-0 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168687 :answer-field/correct 17592186168689 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-9d4f7d2e-5a54-5483-93ff-febe106e9483" :question/id #uuid "9d4f7d2e-5a54-5483-93ff-febe106e9483" :question/math-academy-id "q-127370" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨-x,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2{x}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=-y+1,$ $\,x={e}^{y},$ and the line $y=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/72/728036ffc90e2476017b3102b6279f9c5900f0e7fc58536e76c9aa038eb04f02.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=-x$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2{x}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y+1\le x\le {e}^{y},\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y+1}^{{e}^{y}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{-y+1}^{{e}^{y}}\,dy \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{y}+y-1)\,dy \\  & =-{[{e}^{y}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-[(e+\frac{1}{2}-1)-1] \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-e.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d52f83e4-8134-5921-a35f-e8152b063a24"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d52f83e4-8134-5921-a35f-e8152b063a24" :answer-field/id #uuid "d52f83e4-8134-5921-a35f-e8152b063a24" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e6d825d3-bc21-53d9-9b80-37d93f21f53c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-491c7d85-23b8-5360-a8a5-150039e21ba9" "answer-091bc970-fa77-5e71-85b9-f1ab8c6a0482" "answer-55384a96-bb48-572a-9f44-39ec987e63ac" "answer-e6d825d3-bc21-53d9-9b80-37d93f21f53c" "answer-c4d61b2f-57fc-5cda-b0b0-9b59235e0fb3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-491c7d85-23b8-5360-a8a5-150039e21ba9" :answer/id #uuid "491c7d85-23b8-5360-a8a5-150039e21ba9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-091bc970-fa77-5e71-85b9-f1ab8c6a0482" :answer/id #uuid "091bc970-fa77-5e71-85b9-f1ab8c6a0482" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5{e}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-55384a96-bb48-572a-9f44-39ec987e63ac" :answer/id #uuid "55384a96-bb48-572a-9f44-39ec987e63ac" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e6d825d3-bc21-53d9-9b80-37d93f21f53c" :answer/id #uuid "e6d825d3-bc21-53d9-9b80-37d93f21f53c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}-e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c4d61b2f-57fc-5cda-b0b0-9b59235e0fb3" :answer/id #uuid "c4d61b2f-57fc-5cda-b0b0-9b59235e0fb3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}+2e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-44ac1bd4-9843-582f-80a5-1b691b1d5da4" :question/id #uuid "44ac1bd4-9843-582f-80a5-1b691b1d5da4" :question/math-academy-id "q-127328" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}+y,\,xy+1⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=-y,$ $\,x=\sqrt{y},$ and the line $y=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/2e/2ecabe22395006f0c7ef0a3f914087fa324f4d59c7d7886c18907f824744643e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+y$ and $Q(x,y)=xy+1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y\le x\le \sqrt{y},\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y}^{\sqrt{y}}3x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{-y}^{\sqrt{y}}\,dy \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-19474be3-1fd4-58b1-9c1c-f483db0b1748"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-19474be3-1fd4-58b1-9c1c-f483db0b1748" :answer-field/id #uuid "19474be3-1fd4-58b1-9c1c-f483db0b1748" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-dbf01d52-6bde-5d5c-8f28-24beb09eed98" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3452acaf-89b6-53ae-861d-c8309d517e98" "answer-4b779ef3-0c88-57d7-943a-271c2a83d88c" "answer-38444180-4e68-5f1d-94e7-63374144fcf9" "answer-395d167e-4282-5829-b24d-6655ea33a853" "answer-dbf01d52-6bde-5d5c-8f28-24beb09eed98"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3452acaf-89b6-53ae-861d-c8309d517e98" :answer/id #uuid "3452acaf-89b6-53ae-861d-c8309d517e98" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4b779ef3-0c88-57d7-943a-271c2a83d88c" :answer/id #uuid "4b779ef3-0c88-57d7-943a-271c2a83d88c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{7}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-38444180-4e68-5f1d-94e7-63374144fcf9" :answer/id #uuid "38444180-4e68-5f1d-94e7-63374144fcf9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-395d167e-4282-5829-b24d-6655ea33a853" :answer/id #uuid "395d167e-4282-5829-b24d-6655ea33a853" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dbf01d52-6bde-5d5c-8f28-24beb09eed98" :answer/id #uuid "dbf01d52-6bde-5d5c-8f28-24beb09eed98" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173207 :tutorial/content "There is some nice intuition behind the flux form of Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ with component functions $P$ and $Q$ defined over a region $D.$ So, we have

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form states that the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf F$ inside $D$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D.$

![](images/47/47a81125069be94b4ccda6f228ff1b8253f99595c6f3c4ae0ca710bdb796215f.png)

    

Recall that the divergence (i.e., the microscopic flux) of $\mathbf F$ at a point is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

If we sum (integrate) the divergence at every point over the entire domain $D,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A.
$$

This expression gives us one side of Green's theorem in flux form.

The macroscopic divergence is simply the flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s
$$

Equating the sum of the divergences with the flux, we have

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s.
$$

The flux form of Green's theorem can be summarized in a single picture, as follows:

![](images/0f/0f8ba4b7e853e3b59e8677b0954c3cfae1b9c482750e13a742bd4d45eda8005d.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172181 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$

$$

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-501779b1-729b-5f0b-8f00-ddfd19deba04"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-501779b1-729b-5f0b-8f00-ddfd19deba04" :answer-field/id #uuid "501779b1-729b-5f0b-8f00-ddfd19deba04" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ac21a517-9ce2-51e1-a210-d1342e658153" :answer-field/choices ["answer-84832c07-1cf7-5890-95f5-93379bbcf9e7" "answer-ac21a517-9ce2-51e1-a210-d1342e658153" "answer-a513c7fb-0fe0-56ce-955a-00f68e2e1226" "answer-eb98dc31-4f54-5896-a0d6-e621b6d1e1f7" "answer-036be383-69ad-5c54-97f4-245cc64ebdc5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-84832c07-1cf7-5890-95f5-93379bbcf9e7" :answer/id #uuid "84832c07-1cf7-5890-95f5-93379bbcf9e7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ac21a517-9ce2-51e1-a210-d1342e658153" :answer/id #uuid "ac21a517-9ce2-51e1-a210-d1342e658153" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a513c7fb-0fe0-56ce-955a-00f68e2e1226" :answer/id #uuid "a513c7fb-0fe0-56ce-955a-00f68e2e1226" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eb98dc31-4f54-5896-a0d6-e621b6d1e1f7" :answer/id #uuid "eb98dc31-4f54-5896-a0d6-e621b6d1e1f7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-036be383-69ad-5c54-97f4-245cc64ebdc5" :answer/id #uuid "036be383-69ad-5c54-97f4-245cc64ebdc5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5645d046-8b12-5960-a3e0-e0429413dd27" :question/id #uuid "5645d046-8b12-5960-a3e0-e0429413dd27" :question/math-academy-id "q-127337" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{y}^{7}-x,\,{e}^{3x}+x{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the rectangle with vertices $(-1,-1),(0,-1),(0,1),$ and $(-1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/b2/b25d12781632bcc03576a79e7fbf1b22806fc68e3f521ecd602f1b0732d8d90d.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={y}^{7}-x$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{3x}+x{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 0,\,-1\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+2xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(2xy-1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}y-x)\,{|}_{-1}^{0}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[0-((-1)^{2}y-(-1))]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-y-1)\,dy \\  & =[-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-y]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-\frac{(1)^{2}}{2}-(1))-(-\frac{(-1)^{2}}{2}-(-1)) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-15f3b20c-fcac-5124-a093-6cfd6cef919f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-15f3b20c-fcac-5124-a093-6cfd6cef919f" :answer-field/id #uuid "15f3b20c-fcac-5124-a093-6cfd6cef919f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-783926e4-15e5-52ff-ad59-711ade6b214d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-db270bba-95df-51f5-b9d1-ccab96038132" "answer-783926e4-15e5-52ff-ad59-711ade6b214d" "answer-9ceb053a-ae1f-53f2-9912-d9d9157552fa" "answer-5ebdbb3a-9cd8-57c7-9768-3437a54bb5b2" "answer-1afc0e4b-7ec3-5e04-a320-b09bbb7450d5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-db270bba-95df-51f5-b9d1-ccab96038132" :answer/id #uuid "db270bba-95df-51f5-b9d1-ccab96038132" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-783926e4-15e5-52ff-ad59-711ade6b214d" :answer/id #uuid "783926e4-15e5-52ff-ad59-711ade6b214d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9ceb053a-ae1f-53f2-9912-d9d9157552fa" :answer/id #uuid "9ceb053a-ae1f-53f2-9912-d9d9157552fa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5ebdbb3a-9cd8-57c7-9768-3437a54bb5b2" :answer/id #uuid "5ebdbb3a-9cd8-57c7-9768-3437a54bb5b2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1afc0e4b-7ec3-5e04-a320-b09bbb7450d5" :answer/id #uuid "1afc0e4b-7ec3-5e04-a320-b09bbb7450d5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172305 :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}+2y,\,{x}^{2}+2xy⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{2}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/91/9168d2ed7eeaa5f1dd331a0a986ac7ecfd6b964217a2cb614deb0cdd54437d65.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+2y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+2xy.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}4x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4xy\,{|}_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{x}^{3}\,dx \\  & ={x}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & ={1}^{4}-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168693 :answer-field/correct 17592186168696 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-380026fe-2d4e-5527-8902-7fe90302976f" :question/id #uuid "380026fe-2d4e-5527-8902-7fe90302976f" :question/math-academy-id "q-127302" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨14xy,\,6{x}^{2}y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{3}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/e6/e6f6a5cf9b37fe16f17fe74face946d85b426badf8db710ca4a7ea308a1ff2ec.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=14xy$ and $Q(x,y)=6{x}^{2}y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=14y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =6{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{3}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(14y+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}(14y+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7{y}^{2}+6{x}^{2}y)\,{|}_{0}^{{x}^{3}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7{x}^{6}+6{x}^{5})\,dx \\  & =({x}^{7}+{x}^{6})\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1f5abcf2-857d-5997-8843-79c2143f0e91"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1f5abcf2-857d-5997-8843-79c2143f0e91" :answer-field/id #uuid "1f5abcf2-857d-5997-8843-79c2143f0e91" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-be728807-7dfc-57ad-844a-74242eaae230" :answer-field/choices ["answer-be728807-7dfc-57ad-844a-74242eaae230" "answer-f65df826-8fea-532c-b10f-fd1044e7f4a0" "answer-9e8a5a99-44bd-5b11-83dd-6c16e9e4e40b" "answer-f1954043-6aaa-5ee4-807d-74a521f1268a" "answer-a581e533-3d41-5f80-8a3e-7a4d97fd2b2b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-be728807-7dfc-57ad-844a-74242eaae230" :answer/id #uuid "be728807-7dfc-57ad-844a-74242eaae230" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f65df826-8fea-532c-b10f-fd1044e7f4a0" :answer/id #uuid "f65df826-8fea-532c-b10f-fd1044e7f4a0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9e8a5a99-44bd-5b11-83dd-6c16e9e4e40b" :answer/id #uuid "9e8a5a99-44bd-5b11-83dd-6c16e9e4e40b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f1954043-6aaa-5ee4-807d-74a521f1268a" :answer/id #uuid "f1954043-6aaa-5ee4-807d-74a521f1268a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{6}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a581e533-3d41-5f80-8a3e-7a4d97fd2b2b" :answer/id #uuid "a581e533-3d41-5f80-8a3e-7a4d97fd2b2b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172304 :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨3{x}^{5}+2y,\,3{y}^{2}-{e}^{x}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,1),$ and $(-1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/26/269e3c7f92cee66c78f3226e7c967eb51153503c598d2e4d1e4b56a33e646ac4.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=3{x}^{5}+2y$ and $Q(x,y)=3{y}^{2}-{e}^{x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=15{x}^{4},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =6y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(15{x}^{4}+6y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y}^{y}(15{x}^{4}+6y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[3{x}^{5}+6xy]_{-y}^{y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[(3{y}^{5}+6{y}^{2})-(-3{y}^{5}-6{y}^{2})]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6{y}^{5}+12{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & =[{y}^{6}+4{y}^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+4)-0 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168687 :answer-field/correct 17592186168689 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-9d4f7d2e-5a54-5483-93ff-febe106e9483" :question/id #uuid "9d4f7d2e-5a54-5483-93ff-febe106e9483" :question/math-academy-id "q-127370" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨-x,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2{x}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=-y+1,$ $\,x={e}^{y},$ and the line $y=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/72/728036ffc90e2476017b3102b6279f9c5900f0e7fc58536e76c9aa038eb04f02.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=-x$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2{x}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y+1\le x\le {e}^{y},\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y+1}^{{e}^{y}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{-y+1}^{{e}^{y}}\,dy \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{y}+y-1)\,dy \\  & =-{[{e}^{y}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-[(e+\frac{1}{2}-1)-1] \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-e.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d52f83e4-8134-5921-a35f-e8152b063a24"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d52f83e4-8134-5921-a35f-e8152b063a24" :answer-field/id #uuid "d52f83e4-8134-5921-a35f-e8152b063a24" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e6d825d3-bc21-53d9-9b80-37d93f21f53c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-491c7d85-23b8-5360-a8a5-150039e21ba9" "answer-091bc970-fa77-5e71-85b9-f1ab8c6a0482" "answer-55384a96-bb48-572a-9f44-39ec987e63ac" "answer-e6d825d3-bc21-53d9-9b80-37d93f21f53c" "answer-c4d61b2f-57fc-5cda-b0b0-9b59235e0fb3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-491c7d85-23b8-5360-a8a5-150039e21ba9" :answer/id #uuid "491c7d85-23b8-5360-a8a5-150039e21ba9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-091bc970-fa77-5e71-85b9-f1ab8c6a0482" :answer/id #uuid "091bc970-fa77-5e71-85b9-f1ab8c6a0482" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5{e}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-55384a96-bb48-572a-9f44-39ec987e63ac" :answer/id #uuid "55384a96-bb48-572a-9f44-39ec987e63ac" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e6d825d3-bc21-53d9-9b80-37d93f21f53c" :answer/id #uuid "e6d825d3-bc21-53d9-9b80-37d93f21f53c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}-e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c4d61b2f-57fc-5cda-b0b0-9b59235e0fb3" :answer/id #uuid "c4d61b2f-57fc-5cda-b0b0-9b59235e0fb3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}+2e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-44ac1bd4-9843-582f-80a5-1b691b1d5da4" :question/id #uuid "44ac1bd4-9843-582f-80a5-1b691b1d5da4" :question/math-academy-id "q-127328" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}+y,\,xy+1⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=-y,$ $\,x=\sqrt{y},$ and the line $y=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/2e/2ecabe22395006f0c7ef0a3f914087fa324f4d59c7d7886c18907f824744643e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+y$ and $Q(x,y)=xy+1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y\le x\le \sqrt{y},\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y}^{\sqrt{y}}3x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{-y}^{\sqrt{y}}\,dy \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-19474be3-1fd4-58b1-9c1c-f483db0b1748"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-19474be3-1fd4-58b1-9c1c-f483db0b1748" :answer-field/id #uuid "19474be3-1fd4-58b1-9c1c-f483db0b1748" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-dbf01d52-6bde-5d5c-8f28-24beb09eed98" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3452acaf-89b6-53ae-861d-c8309d517e98" "answer-4b779ef3-0c88-57d7-943a-271c2a83d88c" "answer-38444180-4e68-5f1d-94e7-63374144fcf9" "answer-395d167e-4282-5829-b24d-6655ea33a853" "answer-dbf01d52-6bde-5d5c-8f28-24beb09eed98"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3452acaf-89b6-53ae-861d-c8309d517e98" :answer/id #uuid "3452acaf-89b6-53ae-861d-c8309d517e98" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4b779ef3-0c88-57d7-943a-271c2a83d88c" :answer/id #uuid "4b779ef3-0c88-57d7-943a-271c2a83d88c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{7}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-38444180-4e68-5f1d-94e7-63374144fcf9" :answer/id #uuid "38444180-4e68-5f1d-94e7-63374144fcf9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-395d167e-4282-5829-b24d-6655ea33a853" :answer/id #uuid "395d167e-4282-5829-b24d-6655ea33a853" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dbf01d52-6bde-5d5c-8f28-24beb09eed98" :answer/id #uuid "dbf01d52-6bde-5d5c-8f28-24beb09eed98" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173207 :tutorial/content "There is some nice intuition behind the flux form of Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ with component functions $P$ and $Q$ defined over a region $D.$ So, we have

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form states that the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf F$ inside $D$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D.$

![](images/47/47a81125069be94b4ccda6f228ff1b8253f99595c6f3c4ae0ca710bdb796215f.png)

    

Recall that the divergence (i.e., the microscopic flux) of $\mathbf F$ at a point is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

If we sum (integrate) the divergence at every point over the entire domain $D,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A.
$$

This expression gives us one side of Green's theorem in flux form.

The macroscopic divergence is simply the flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s
$$

Equating the sum of the divergences with the flux, we have

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s.
$$

The flux form of Green's theorem can be summarized in a single picture, as follows:

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)-{x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2y.$ So,

$$

$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4y+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(2x-4y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[{x}^{2}-4yx]_{-1}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[({1}^{2}-4y(1))-((-1)^{2}-4y(-1))]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}-8y\,dy \\  & =-4{y}^{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(-4(-1)^{2}) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/f7/f7400787e09600d370fa5c554e616fad6ba3a126a09725cfb236502f81a7e70e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y{e}^{y}-4xy$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)-4x{y}^{3}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-12x{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4y-12x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4y-12x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-4xy-6{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\,{|}_{0}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[(-4(1)^{2}y-6(1)^{2}{y}^{2})-0]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-4y-6{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & =[-2{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-2(1)^{2}-2(1)^{3})-(-2(-1)^{2}-2(-1)^{3}) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-621adbef-22f1-5cf5-b77b-1bf6fb7f602e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-501779b1-729b-5f0b-8f00-ddfd19deba04" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/b2/b25d12781632bcc03576a79e7fbf1b22806fc68e3f521ecd602f1b0732d8d90d.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={y}^{7}-x$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{3x}+x{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 0,\,-1\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+2xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(2xy-1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}y-x)\,{|}_{-1}^{0}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[0-((-1)^{2}y-(-1))]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-y-1)\,dy \\  & =[-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-y]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-\frac{(1)^{2}}{2}-(1))-(-\frac{(-1)^{2}}{2}-(-1)) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-5645d046-8b12-5960-a3e0-e0429413dd27" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-15f3b20c-fcac-5124-a093-6cfd6cef919f" :answer-field/id #uuid We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+2y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+2xy.$ Therefore,

"question-44ac1bd4-9843-582f-80a5-1b691b1d5da4"] [17592186173207 :tutorial/content "There is some nice intuition behind the flux form of Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ with component functions $P$ and $Q$ defined over a region $D.$ So, we have

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form states that the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf F$ inside $D$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D.$

![](images/47/47a81125069be94b4ccda6f228ff1b8253f99595c6f3c4ae0ca710bdb796215f.png)

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

If we sum (integrate) the divergence at every point over the entire domain $D,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A.
$$

This expression gives us one side of Green's theorem in flux form.

The macroscopic divergence is simply the flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s
$$

Equating the sum of the divergences with the flux, we have

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s.
$$

[{:db/id 17592186172099 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "629dd9d1-1c53-5a04-97bf-5799e71b9573" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Flux Across Other Type I and Type II Regions"}] :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle -3xy^2 , \: y+\cos x \right\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0), (2,2),$ and $(-2,2).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/aa/aa822f0b9259d6d9eb5c6f439588e70d4b9bee16b2b868fae36c7cbac72d3c3f.png)

We have that $P(x,y) = -3xy^2$ and $Q(x,y) = y+\cos x .$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D = \left\{(x,y) :  -y \leq x \leq y, \, 0 \leq y \leq 2 \right\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-3{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y}^{y}(-3{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{y}^{2}+1)[x]_{-y}^{y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{y}^{2}+1)(y-(-y))\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{y}^{2}+1)\cdot 2y\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-6{y}^{3}+2y)\,dy \\  & =[-6\cdot \frac{{y}^{4}}{4}+2\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =[-\frac{3{y}^{4}}{2}+{y}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =(-24+4)-0 \\  & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186172304 :question/id #uuid "5f0fa3f4-0fcf-5a8c-888e-2010c07d0c94" :question/math-academy-id "q-126814" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172099 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "629dd9d1-1c53-5a04-97bf-5799e71b9573" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Flux Across Other Type I and Type II Regions"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8139aeea-718b-5375-803a-93347bbc782c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186168688} {:answer/id #uuid "82c8004a-2ac3-5893-a60f-73d6f8e77a9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186168689} {:answer/id #uuid "c2f9605f-4b60-5e53-b7a3-b64df5b69052" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186168690} {:answer/id #uuid "1be0a1ca-8486-5941-bb49-31449f0eb29e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186168691} {:answer/id #uuid "5d79f02e-fcd8-5711-9839-d7029ccbd6a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186168692}] :answer-field/id #uuid "4a5efa42-6a58-5189-86a4-80345f8c4752" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186168687}] :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

through $C$ as a repeated integral." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A,

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.

![](images/02/02964b07e45daba2d560fa16d34bcc92ddb8d0e0e83f644f8284dbe9d4b4557b.png)

$$

$$
D = \{(x,y) :  -1\leq x\leq 1, \, -3\leq y \leq 0\}
$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186050793} {:db/id 17592186051070} {:db/id 17592186172308 :question/id #uuid "eeef3f59-4373-5478-9f71-3d8588687de5" :question/math-academy-id "q-127070" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172100 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d5c7e707-c978-566d-8a69-98c84c7eb53e" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing Flux as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem in Flux Form"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "92524a07-a3e1-5079-a783-a2c3939a0144" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2(x - y)" :db/id 17592186168712} {:answer/id #uuid "0e61397f-92af-5d0d-b6d9-a91fcccf055b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2(x + y)" :db/id 17592186168713} {:answer/id #uuid "1cfac84a-5548-5538-b921-90b81934181d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}(x^{2} + y^{2})" :db/id 17592186168714} {:answer/id #uuid "64e84502-cab6-5b40-ac60-48ec2879b68c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2(y - x)" :db/id 17592186168715} {:answer/id #uuid "6802eb91-025c-5c5c-abc5-05ce7e442b6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}(x^{2} - y^{2})" :db/id 17592186168716}] :answer-field/id #uuid "6725b75c-c66c-52af-8566-302236c9d990" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186168711}] :question/problem "According to the flux form of Green's theorem, the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle \sin(\pi y) - x , \: \cos(\pi x) + 2xy \right\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the square with vertices $(0,-1), (2,-1), (2,1),$ and $(0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/2f/2f3374de4a29c62587a79f6286dfe788e64c37e09e9d9b83b3a67b4dac10dc21.png)

We have that $P(x,y) = \sin(\pi y) - x$ and $Q(x,y) = \cos(\pi x) + 2xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D = \left\{(x,y) :  0 \leq x \leq 2, \, -1 \leq y \leq 1 \right\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}-x)\,{|}_{0}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({2}^{2}-2)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2\,dy \\  & =2y\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2(1)-2(-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}

"b533c8b3-90f2-54ee-ae35-a98929d6ba6e" :step/math-academy-id 35837 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173009}} {:db/id 17592186173012 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173207 :tutorial/content "There is some nice intuition behind the flux form of Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ with component functions $P$ and $Q$ defined over a region $D.$ So, we have

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form states that the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf F$ inside $D$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D.$

![](images/47/47a81125069be94b4ccda6f228ff1b8253f99595c6f3c4ae0ca710bdb796215f.png)

Recall that the divergence (i.e., the microscopic flux) of $\mathbf F$ at a point is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

If we sum (integrate) the divergence at every point over the entire domain $D,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A.
$$

This expression gives us one side of Green's theorem in flux form.

The macroscopic divergence is simply the flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s
$$

Equating the sum of the divergences with the flux, we have

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s.
$$

The flux form of Green's theorem can be summarized in a single picture, as follows:

![](images/0f/0f8ba4b7e853e3b59e8677b0954c3cfae1b9c482750e13a742bd4d45eda8005d.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "9016229b-93aa-58fc-857c-2a2d3f337ca4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5862 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind Green's Theorem in Flux Form"} :step/id #uuid "e5c29654-0b83-51e0-a3d0-c6fbf08c8f2d" :step/math-academy-id 35877 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173010}} {:db/id 17592186173013 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173208 :tutorial/content "Green's theorem allows us to write line integrals as double integrals, and we've seen how Green's theorem simplifies circulation calculations. Even more, Green's theorem can also be used to simplify flux calculations!

To see how, we first recall that the flux of $\mathbf{F}(x,y) =  P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\mathbf j$ across $C$ can be calculated as follows:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s= \oint\limits_C P\, \textrm{d}y -Q\, \textrm{d}x
$$

where $C$ is closed and $\mathbf n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Now, let's set $M= -Q$ and $N=P$. Then, by the circulation form of Green's theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x & ={∮}_{C}N\,\text{d}y+M\,\text{d}x \\  & ={∮}_{C}M\,\text{d}x+N\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂N}{∂x}-\frac{∂M}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}-(-\frac{∂Q}{∂y}))\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we've obtained the **Green's theorem in flux form**, which we restate below:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \iint\limits_D \left(\dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} +\dfrac{\partial  Q}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A
$$

Now, recall that the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F =  \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

Therefore, we can also write Green's theorem in flux form as

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form allows us to convert a flux line integral into an equivalent double integral." :tutorial/id #uuid "7f3b4b70-8b58-53d1-bc8d-a42daddfab4d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5868 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "528120c2-edf7-5b3d-a8d3-0b481b460d90" :step/math-academy-id 35900 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173012}}] :activity/title "Green's Theorem in Flux Form" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172181} {:db/id 17592186173013 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173208 :tutorial/content "Green's theorem allows us to write line integrals as double integrals, and we've seen how Green's theorem simplifies circulation calculations. :step/next {:db/id 17592186173009}} {:db/id 17592186173012 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173207 :tutorial/content "There is some nice intuition behind the flux form of Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ with component functions $P$ and $Q$ defined over a region $D.$ So, we have

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form states that the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf F$ inside $D$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D.$

![](images/47/47a81125069be94b4ccda6f228ff1b8253f99595c6f3c4ae0ca710bdb796215f.png)

Recall that the divergence (i.e., the microscopic flux) of $\mathbf F$ at a point is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

If we sum (integrate) the divergence at every point over the entire domain $D,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A.
$$

This expression gives us one side of Green's theorem in flux form.

The macroscopic divergence is simply the flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s
$$

Equating the sum of the divergences with the flux, we have

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s.
$$

The flux form of Green's theorem can be summarized in a single picture, as follows:

![](images/0f/0f8ba4b7e853e3b59e8677b0954c3cfae1b9c482750e13a742bd4d45eda8005d.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "9016229b-93aa-58fc-857c-2a2d3f337ca4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5862 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind Green's Theorem in Flux Form"} :step/id #uuid "e5c29654-0b83-51e0-a3d0-c6fbf08c8f2d" :step/math-academy-id 35877 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173010}} {:db/id 17592186173207 :tutorial/content "There is some nice intuition behind the flux form of Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ with component functions $P$ and $Q$ defined over a region $D.$ So, we have

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form states that the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf F$ inside $D$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D.$

![](images/47/47a81125069be94b4ccda6f228ff1b8253f99595c6f3c4ae0ca710bdb796215f.png)

Recall that the divergence (i.e., the microscopic flux) of $\mathbf F$ at a point is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

If we sum (integrate) the divergence at every point over the entire domain $D,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A.
$$

This expression gives us one side of Green's theorem in flux form.

The macroscopic divergence is simply the flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s
$$

Equating the sum of the divergences with the flux, we have

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s.
$$

The flux form of Green's theorem can be summarized in a single picture, as follows:

![](images/0f/0f8ba4b7e853e3b59e8677b0954c3cfae1b9c482750e13a742bd4d45eda8005d.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "9016229b-93aa-58fc-857c-2a2d3f337ca4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5862 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind Green's Theorem in Flux Form"} {:db/id 17592186173208 :tutorial/content "Green's theorem allows us to write line integrals as double integrals, and we've seen how Green's theorem simplifies circulation calculations. Even more, Green's theorem can also be used to simplify flux calculations!

To see how, we first recall that the flux of $\mathbf{F}(x,y) =  P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\mathbf j$ across $C$ can be calculated as follows:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s= \oint\limits_C P\, \textrm{d}y -Q\, \textrm{d}x
$$

where $C$ is closed and $\mathbf n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Now, let's set $M= -Q$ and $N=P$. Then, by the circulation form of Green's theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x & ={∮}_{C}N\,\text{d}y+M\,\text{d}x \\  & ={∮}_{C}M\,\text{d}x+N\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂N}{∂x}-\frac{∂M}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}-(-\frac{∂Q}{∂y}))\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we've obtained the **Green's theorem in flux form**, which we restate below:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \iint\limits_D \left(\dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} +\dfrac{\partial  Q}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A
$$

Now, recall that the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F =  \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

Therefore, we can also write Green's theorem in flux form as

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form allows us to convert a flux line integral into an equivalent double integral." :tutorial/id #uuid "7f3b4b70-8b58-53d1-bc8d-a42daddfab4d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5868 Sciences II" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.
The course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ with component functions $P$ and $Q$ defined over a region $D.$ So, we have

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form states that the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf F$ inside $D$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D.$

![](images/47/47a81125069be94b4ccda6f228ff1b8253f99595c6f3c4ae0ca710bdb796215f.png)

Recall that the divergence (i.e., the microscopic flux) of $\mathbf F$ at a point is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

If we sum (integrate) the divergence at every point over the entire domain $D,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A.
$$

This expression gives us one side of Green's theorem in flux form.

The macroscopic divergence is simply the flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s
$$

Equating the sum of the divergences with the flux, we have

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s.
$$

The flux form of Green's theorem can be summarized in a single picture, as follows:

![](images/0f/0f8ba4b7e853e3b59e8677b0954c3cfae1b9c482750e13a742bd4d45eda8005d.png)" 17592186045417] [17592186173207 1065 5862 17592186045417] [17592186173207 1066 #uuid "9016229b-93aa-58fc-857c-2a2d3f337ca4" 17592186045417] [17592186173207 1067 "Intuition Behind Green's Theorem in Flux Form" 17592186045417] [17592186173208 1064 "Green's theorem allows us to write line integrals as double integrals, and we've seen how Green's theorem simplifies circulation calculations. Even more, Green's theorem can also be used to simplify flux calculations!

To see how, we first recall that the flux of $\mathbf{F}(x,y) =  P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\mathbf j$ across $C$ can be calculated as follows:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s= \oint\limits_C P\, \textrm{d}y -Q\, \textrm{d}x
$$

where $C$ is closed and $\mathbf n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Now, let's set $M= -Q$ and $N=P$. Then, by the circulation form of Green's theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x & ={∮}_{C}N\,\text{d}y+M\,\text{d}x \\  & ={∮}_{C}M\,\text{d}x+N\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂N}{∂x}-\frac{∂M}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}-(-\frac{∂Q}{∂y}))\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we've obtained the **Green's theorem in flux form**, which we restate below:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \iint\limits_D \left(\dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} +\dfrac{\partial  Q}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A
$$

Now, recall that the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F =  \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

Therefore, we can also write Green's theorem in flux form as

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form allows us to convert a flux line integral into an equivalent double integral." 17592186045417] [17592186173208 1065 5868 17592186045417] [17592186173208 1066 #uuid "7f3b4b70-8b58-53d1-bc8d-a42daddfab4d" 17592186045417] [17592186173208 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417]]}
